title: History of Morocco
wiki_lead:
The history of human habitation in Morocco extends back to the Lower Paleolithic, with evidence of hominin activity at Thomas Quarry I in Casablanca dating to around 1.3 million years ago and securely dated hominin fossils from the same locality dating to around 773,000 years ago. Much later, Morocco formed part of the Iberomaurusian cultural sphere, represented by sites such as Taforalt. The region later saw the establishment of Mauretania and other ancient Berber kingdoms, followed by the foundation of the Moroccan state under the Idrisid dynasty and the rise of successive Islamic dynasties, culminating in the establishment of the Alawi dynasty, which has ruled Morocco since the 17th century and remains the country's reigning dynasty today.
The recorded history of Morocco begins with the Phoenician colonization of the Moroccan coast between the 8th and 6th centuries BCE, although the area was inhabited by indigenous Berbers for some two thousand years before that. In the 5th century BCE, the city-state of Carthage extended its hegemony over the coastal areas. They remained there until the late 3rd century BCE, while the hinterland was ruled by indigenous monarchs. Indigenous Berber monarchs ruled the territory from the 3rd century BCE until 40 CE, when it was annexed to the Roman Empire. In the mid-5th century CE, it was overrun by Vandals, before being recovered by the Byzantine Empire in the 6th century.
The region was conquered by the Muslims in the early 8th century CE but broke away from the Umayyad Caliphate following the Berber Revolt of 740. Half a century later, the Moroccan state was established by the Idrisid dynasty. The Idrisids were succeeded by the Almoravid dynasty, the Almohad dynasty, the Marinid dynasty and the Wattasid dynasty. The Saadi dynasty then ruled Morocco from the 16th to the 17th century, followed by the Alawi dynasty from 1667 onward.

Prehistoric Morocco

Archaeological excavations have demonstrated the presence in Morocco of people ancestral to Homo sapiens, as well as earlier human species. In 2026, researchers described hominin fossils from the Grotte à Hominidés at Thomas Quarry I in Casablanca, securely dated to approximately 773,000 years ago. The fossilized remains of an early human ancestor, dated to around 400,000 years ago, were discovered in Salé in 1971.
Remains of early Homo sapiens were excavated at Jebel Irhoud in 1991. In 2017, the remains were dated using modern techniques to at least 300,000 years ago, making them the oldest known examples of Homo sapiens discovered.
In 2007, small perforated seashell beads dating to approximately 82,000 years ago were discovered at Taforalt. The finds represent some of the earliest known evidence of personal adornment.
During the Mesolithic period (c. 20,000–5000 years ago), the geography of Morocco resembled a savanna rather than the present arid landscape. Although little is known about settlements in Morocco during this period, excavations elsewhere in the Maghreb suggest an abundance of game and forests suitable for Mesolithic hunter-gatherer societies, including those associated with the Capsian culture.
During the Neolithic period, which followed the Mesolithic, the savanna was inhabited by hunters and herders. The culture of these Neolithic communities flourished until the region began to desiccate after 5000 BCE due to climatic changes. The coastal regions of present-day Morocco during the early Neolithic shared in the Cardium pottery culture common across the Mediterranean region. Archaeological evidence suggests that the domestication of cattle and the cultivation of crops occurred in the region during this period.
During the Chalcolithic period (Copper Age), the Beaker culture reached the northern coast of Morocco.

grok_lead: The history of Morocco encompasses the prehistoric habitation of the region by indigenous Berber (Amazigh) peoples, ancient coastal settlements influenced by Phoenician traders from the 12th to 6th centuries BCE, Roman annexation as the province of Mauretania Tingitana in 40 CE, and subsequent Vandal and Byzantine occupations before the Arab Muslim conquests of the 7thâ8th centuries CE. Following these early phases, Morocco developed as an autonomous center of Islamic power, with the Idrisid dynasty (788â974) establishing the first independent Muslim state in the western Maghreb, rejecting full subordination to the Abbasid Caliphate in Baghdad. Successive Berber-led dynasties, including the Almoravids (c. 1040â1147) and Almohads (c. 1121â1269), unified the territory, expanded into al-Andalus (Muslim Iberia), and controlled trans-Saharan trade routes vital for gold, salt, and slaves, fostering economic prosperity and architectural achievements like the Koutoubia Mosque in Marrakech. The Marinids (c. 1244â1465), Wattasids (c. 1472â1554), Saadians (c. 1549â1659), and Alaouites (from 1631) maintained Morocco's sovereignty amid Ottoman expansions elsewhere in North Africa, leveraging geographic barriers like the Atlas Mountains and a tradition of jihad against external threats to preserve dynastic rule. European incursions intensified in the 19th century, leading to the establishment of French and Spanish protectorates in 1912, which divided the country and sparked resistance movements such as the Rif War (1921â1926) under Abd el-Krim, highlighting Berber tribal autonomy and anti-colonial fervor. Independence was achieved on March 2, 1956, through negotiations ending the French protectorate, followed shortly by Spanish withdrawal from most territories, restoring full sovereignty under Sultan Mohammed V of the Alaouite line, who transitioned to king amid nationalist pressures and the suppression of internal dissent. Defining characteristics include Morocco's role as a cultural crossroadsâblending Berber, Arab, Andalusian, and sub-Saharan elementsâevident in institutions like the University of al-Qarawiyyin (founded 859 CE, the world's oldest continuously operating degree-granting university) and its strategic position enabling control over Mediterranean-Atlantic trade while resisting full integration into larger empires. Controversies persist over territorial claims, such as the Western Sahara dispute since 1975, rooted in pre-colonial suzerainty but contested internationally, underscoring tensions between monarchical centralization and regional autonomy.
